notes:
I now have substantial material to compile verse-by-verse notes on Psalm 16. Here are my findings:

---

## Psalm 16 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Title: "A Miktam of David"

- **The term "Miktam"** is uncertain. It is commonly understood as "golden" (from *kethem*, gold), suggesting a precious or golden psalm. Others link it to a root meaning "to cover," and since Psalms 16, 56–60 (all bearing this title) were written from times of peril, some think it means a "secret" or "silent" psalm for a time of crisis. The LXX renders it "a pillar inscription" (*stelographia*). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-16/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/16.htm

- **Spurgeon** calls the psalm a "golden mystery" whose key is given by the Holy Spirit through Peter in Acts 2:25–31: "David speaketh concerning HIM." — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps016.php (search excerpt)

---

### v. 1 — "Preserve me, O God, for in You I take refuge."

- **Traditional reading (Pulpit)**: David asks God to keep him, guard him, protect him in body and soul. He is not necessarily threatened by any special danger; he simply calls on God to continue his protecting care. "In thee, and in thee only … therefore to thee only do I look for protection." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/16.htm

- **Guzik (Enduring Word)**: David wrote from a time of trouble, yet the tone is "settled joy," not despair. The plea to be preserved is grounded in trust: "for in You I put my trust." Trapp calls this "a most powerful plea, for to trust God is the highest honour we can do him." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-16/

- **Ellicott** notes the verb is in the preterite (past tense): "I have found refuge in thee" — the trust is an already-established reality, not a new decision. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/16.htm

- **Spurgeon (Baptist)**: Reads this as Christ's own prayer of faith. In his sermon "Christ's Prayer and Plea," Spurgeon treats the entire psalm as spoken by Christ. — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps016.php (search excerpt); https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalms_-_sermons_by_spurgeon

- **Augustine (Catholic/Patristic)**: Interprets v.1 as Christ speaking "in the character of the human nature He assumed" — "Our King in this Psalm speaks … of whom the royal title at the time of His passion was eminently set forth." — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801016.htm

- **John Piper (Reformed Baptist)**: Notes that the petition "Preserve me" shapes the whole psalm. David moves from petition to confidence as he exults in what God is for him. — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-path-to-full-and-lasting-pleasure (search excerpt)

---

### v. 2 — "I said to the LORD, 'You are my Lord; apart from You I have no good thing.'"

- **Pulpit Commentary**: The Hebrew *tobah* means "prosperity" or "happiness," not moral "goodness." The sense is: "I have no happiness beside (or apart from) God." This reading is supported by Ewald, Hengstenberg, Cheyne, the Speaker's Commentary, and the RV. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/16.htm

- **Ellicott** agrees: "'My good' … equals 'happiness,' not 'conduct.'" The consensus of ancient versions favours the first person: "I said to Jehovah, Thou art my Lord, I have no good besides thee." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/16.htm

- **Guzik**: David happily declared Yahweh as his master (*Adonai*). He knew his very best was "nothing apart from God" — both because his goodness was a gift from God and because it was of small value without relationship with God. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-16/

- **Piper**: "You are my Lord, and you are my good. That is, as my Lord you govern all the good that comes to me, and you are the good that comes to me." — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-lord-governs-my-good-and-is-my-good (search excerpt)

---

### v. 3 — "As for the saints in the land, they are the excellence in whom all my delight resides."

- **Guzik**: David delighted in the people of God despite all their failings. This is a practical test: "Do you love other Christians? … Those who love the Lord will love the company of those who also love him" (Boice). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-16/

- **Pulpit Commentary** takes a different reading: The Hebrew is better rendered "It is for the saints" — David's prosperity is granted him *for the advantage of the saints*. "I hold it in trust for them" (Kay), especially for "the inner circle of the excellent ones." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/16.htm

- **Ellicott**: With emendation, the verse runs: "And of the saints who are in the earth, they are the excellent in whom is all my delight." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/16.htm

- **Augustine** reads this Christologically: "To the saints who have placed their hope in the land of the living, the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem … He has wonderfully fulfilled all My wishes in them." — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801016.htm

- **Precept Austin / Today in the Word**: "The king delighted to worship with other believers who thirsted after God in the same way." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalms_-_today_in_the_word

---

### v. 4 — "Sorrows will multiply to those who chase other gods. I will not pour out their libations of blood, or speak their names with my lips."

- **Pulpit Commentary**: This is "the only note of sadness in the entire psalm," inserted to add force by contrast to the joyous v.5. Those who "hasten after" (or "wed themselves to," cf. Exodus 2:16) another god will find multiplied sorrows. "Drink offerings of blood" is probably metaphorical — drink offerings as hateful as if they had been of blood (cf. Isaiah 66:3), since actual blood libations are scarcely attested. The Law forbade speaking the names of foreign gods (Exodus 23:13; Deuteronomy 12:3). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/16.htm

- **Ellicott**: Notes an "evident allusion to the curse on Eve in Genesis 3:16" in the phrase "multiply their sorrows." The verb rendered "hasten" means "to buy a wife," suggesting the psalmist had the prophetic figure of idolatry as adultery in mind. The "libations of blood" seem to refer to "ghastly rites of Moloch and Chemosh." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/16.htm

- **Guzik**: David knew life lived for God was not easy, but life lived for another god was even more difficult — the attitude of Peter in John 6:66–69: "Lord, to whom shall we go?" — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-16/

- **Augustine**: Reads v.4 as Christ speaking about the infirmities of the saints being multiplied "not for their destruction, but that they might long for the Physician." "I will not gather together their assemblies by blood" means the assemblies shall not be carnal, nor gathered by animal sacrifice. — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801016.htm

---

### v. 5 — "The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; You have made my lot secure."

- **Pulpit Commentary**: God had said to Aaron, "I am thy Part and thine Inheritance" (Numbers 18:20). David claims the same priestly privilege. A man's "cup" in Scripture is his lot or condition in life (Psalm 11:6; 23:5). "Thou maintainest my lot" means God makes it firm and sure. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/16.htm

- **Ellicott**: The poet, "whom we must imagine exiled from his actual inheritance in Canaan, consoles, and more than consoles himself, with the sublime thought that this 'better part' could not be taken away." Quoting Perowne: "What must not he possess who possesses the possessor of all!" — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/16.htm

- **Guzik**: As the youngest son, David could expect no family inheritance; yet God was his portion. This is a picture of contentment: "He is content with what God has given him." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-16/

- **Piper (Reformed Baptist)**: "If there are a hundred portions of food and drink spread out on the table, and one of them is the Lord himself — he is my choice. Nothing satisfies … the way he does. He is my greatest good." — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-path-to-full-and-lasting-pleasure (search excerpt)

---

### v. 6 — "The lines of my boundary have fallen in pleasant places; surely my inheritance is delightful."

- **Pulpit Commentary**: The "lines" are the measuring cords by which allotments of land were distributed (Deuteronomy 32:9; Joshua 17:5). These have fallen to David "in pleasant places" — in Jerusalem and its vicinity. His earthly lot is "delightsome" to him. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/16.htm

- **Ellicott**: The lines "fall" possibly because after measurement, portions were distributed by lot (Joshua 17:5; Micah 2:5). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/16.htm

- **Guzik**: The language speaks of a "good inheritance" from a good God. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-16/

- **Augustine**: Reads this as Christ speaking: "The boundaries of my possession have fallen in Your glory as it were by lot, like as God is the possession of the Priests and Levites." — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801016.htm

---

### v. 7 — "I will bless the LORD who counsels me; even at night my conscience instructs me."

- **Pulpit Commentary**: God has become David's "Counsellor" (cf. Psalm 32:8). The "reins" (kidneys) are, in Hebrew thought, the seat of feeling and emotion. David is "instructed" or "stimulated" (Hengstenberg) to bless God by feelings of affection and gratitude that stir within him as he lies awake at night. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/16.htm

- **Ellicott**: "Conscience echoes the voice of God." The Hebrew word for "instruct" comes from a root meaning "bind," including the sense of obligation: "Once heard, the Divine monition becomes a law to the good man." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/16.htm

- **Guzik**: David's heart was instructed first by God and His Word, so his heart could then instruct him — an example of the transformation of thinking in Romans 12:1–2. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-16/

- **Piper**: God is not only David's refuge, treasure, and sovereign, but also his counselor — "This is not a small or insignificant add-on. It colors everything else." — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-path-to-full-and-lasting-pleasure (search excerpt)

- **Constable (Dispensational)**: "This is the first of many references to blessing or praising the Lord in the Book of Psalms." David received special revelation about his deliverance. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-16.html (search excerpt)

---

### v. 8 — "I have set the LORD always before me. Because He is at my right hand, I will not be shaken."

- **Pulpit Commentary**: David has "brought himself to realize the continual presence of God, alike in happiness and in trouble." God at his "right hand" means God is close, ready to protect and save — therefore David "shall not be moved." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/16.htm

- **Ellicott**: The image is "a military one: the shield of the right-hand comrade is a protection to the man beside him" (cf. Psalm 109:31; 110:5; 121:5). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/16.htm

- **Guzik**: This speaks of a decision David made — to put God first, to make God always his focus and perspective. "In the ultimate sense, only Jesus did this perfectly." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-16/

- **Piper**: By v.8, David's petition of v.1 has been transformed into confidence: "I will not be shaken … My petition has become my confidence. I have moved from asking to affirming." — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-path-to-full-and-lasting-pleasure (search excerpt)

- **Spurgeon**: Applies this entirely to Christ: "Jesus is to be viewed as our exemplar; to recognize the presence of the Lord is the duty of every believer." Christ's faith "could discern beforehand the continuance of divine support … in such a degree that he should never be moved from the accomplishment of his purpose of redeeming his people." — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps016.php (search excerpt)

- **Augustine**: "But coming into things that pass away, I removed not My eye from Him who abides ever, foreseeing this, that to Him I should return after passing through the things temporal." — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801016.htm

---

### v. 9 — "Therefore my heart is glad and my tongue rejoices; my body also will dwell securely."

- **Pulpit Commentary**: "Heart" (inner being), "glory" (soul/spirit, cf. Genesis 49:6), and "flesh" (body) — the whole complex man — rests secure. The thought of God's continual presence causes gladness in all three aspects of David's being. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/16.htm

- **Ellicott**: Notes that "glory" (Hebrew *khabôd*) may originally have been *khabed* ("liver" or "heart"). The LXX paraphrases it as "tongue," which is how Acts 2:25 quotes it. "In 'heart, soul, flesh,' the poet comprises the whole living man." The true rendering of "rest in hope" is "rest in security." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/16.htm

- **Guzik**: This verse describes benefits of David's life commitment. The "therefore" links the gladness to the decision in v.8 to set the LORD always before him. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-16/

- **Piper**: "Petition for preservation leads to exultation in God as refuge, and treasure, and sovereign, and counselor, which leads to unshaken confidence that he will be preserved, which leads to deep and pervasive joy." — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-path-to-full-and-lasting-pleasure (search excerpt)

---

### v. 10 — "For You will not abandon my soul to Sheol, nor will You let Your Holy One see decay."

This is the most discussed verse in the psalm, and the point where Protestant traditions show the clearest differences in interpretive approach.

#### Traditional / Mainstream Protestant Reading

- **Pulpit Commentary**: David's confidence in a future life "is beyond that exhibited by Job." Job hopes he may one day experience a "change" (Job 14:14); David is *certain* his soul will not be left in Sheol. Sheol is to him an "intermediate state." On "Holy One" — the Hebrew text has the plural ("thy holy ones"), but the majority of manuscripts, all ancient versions, and the *Keri* (revised Hebrew text) have the singular, agreeing with Acts 2:27, 31 and Acts 13:35. "Certainly he would not have spoken of himself as 'God's holy one.'" On "corruption" vs. "the pit" — the LXX has *diaphthoran* (corruption), and the rendering "the pit" is "quite gratuitous." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/16.htm

- **Guzik (Pentecostal/Charismatic)**: David "spoke beyond himself." In one sense David was God's holy one, but "in a greater and more literal sense, only Jesus Christ fulfills this in His resurrection." Peter on Pentecost perceived that these words went beyond David, whose body had long decayed. The resurrection was "absolutely inevitable" because "it is incomprehensible that God's Holy One should be bound by death." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-16/

#### Baptist (Spurgeon's Christological Reading)

- **Spurgeon** reads the entire psalm, including v.10, as Christ speaking: "Our Lord Jesus was not disappointed in his hope. He declared his Father's faithfulness in the words, 'thou wilt not leave my soul in hell,' and that faithfulness was proven on the resurrection morning." Christ "in soul and body was pre-eminently God's 'Holy One'" and "was loosed from the pains of death, because it was not possible that he should be holden of it." This becomes "noble encouragement to all the saints; die they must, but rise they shall." — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps016.php (search excerpt)

#### Reformed Baptist (Piper)

- **Piper** reads v.10 as David's confidence in bodily preservation through death: "When he said, 'Preserve me, O God,' ultimately, he meant: Don't let me be lost in death. Don't let me be shaken from the realm of the living. Keep me — body and soul — forever." He sees the preservation David asks for as not just deliverance *from* death but preservation *through* death. — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-path-to-full-and-lasting-pleasure (search excerpt)

#### Dispensational (Constable)

- **Constable** argues that David "had received a special revelation from the Lord that he would not die then, but would escape from whatever distress he was enduring." David did not mean he would live forever; "He only meant that he would not die then." What David was confident God would do for him (postpone death), God did for Christ differently (resurrection). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-16.html (search excerpt)

#### Modern Scholarship / Critical View (Ellicott)

- **Ellicott** argues that the Hebrew *shachath* means "a pit" (from a root meaning "to sink in"), not "corruption" (as if from *shakhath*, "to destroy"). "To be left to Sheôl" and "to see the pit" are synonyms for "to die." The meaning is that "Jehovah will not abandon His beloved to death." Yet he acknowledges "the first faint scintillation of that light of immortality" in the psalm. The use in Acts 2 "is justified." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/16.htm

#### Catholic / Patristic Reading

- **Augustine** reads v.10 as entirely Christological: "For You will neither give My soul for a possession to those parts below. Neither will You suffer that sanctified body, whereby others are to be also sanctified, to see corruption." The psalm is Christ speaking of His own resurrection. — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801016.htm

- **Catholic Answers**: "Peter and Paul speak of Psalm 16 (15) when referring to Jesus Christ's death and Resurrection and the salvation his sacrifice would bring." The psalm "attains its full meaning in the light of the New Testament." — https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/psalms (search excerpt)

---

### v. 11 — "You have made known to me the path of life; You will fill me with joy in Your presence, with eternal pleasures at Your right hand."

- **Pulpit Commentary**: "The path of life" is "the path which leads to the Source and Centre of all life, even God himself — the way to heaven, in contrast with corruption and Sheol." "In thy presence is fulness of joy" — literally, "satiety of joy — enough, and more than enough, to satisfy the extremest cravings of the human heart." "At thy right hand; rather, in thy right hand — ready for bestowal on thy saints. Are pleasures for evermore. An inexhaustible store, which may be drawn upon for ever." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/16.htm

- **Ellicott**: The triplet in the Hebrew reads: "Thou wilt show me the path of life, / In thy presence fulness and joy, / At thy right hand pleasures for evermore." It is "another image for the same thought which dominates the psalm — the thought of the happiness of being with God." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/16.htm

- **Guzik**: The path of life is enjoyed both now and in eternity. "In Your presence is fullness of joy" — David could experience this now (in the context of his gladness and rejoicing), but would ultimately receive it in God's more immediate presence. Peter quoted these lines at Pentecost to show that Jesus was rewarded, not punished, for His work on the cross. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-16/

- **Spurgeon** on v.11 (via Trapp): "Here is as much said as can be, but words are too weak to utter it. For quality there is in heaven joy and pleasures; for quantity, a fulness, a torrent whereat they drink without let or loathing; for constancy, it is at God's right hand … and for perpetuity it is for evermore. Heaven's joys are without measure, mixture, or end." — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps016.php (search excerpt)

- **Piper**: "Because God has been his portion here … his confidence is unshaken that God will be all of this perfected forever. This is the final preservation David was hoping for in verse 1." — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-path-to-full-and-lasting-pleasure (search excerpt)

- **Augustine**: "You will fill them with joy, that they should seek nothing further, when they shall see You face to face; in whom because I am, You will fill Me. Pleasure is at Your right hand even to the end." — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801016.htm

- **Kidner** (cited by Guzik): "The refugee of verse 1 finds himself an heir, and his inheritance beyond all imagining and all exploring." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-16/

---

## Summary of Key Differences Among Traditions

| Issue | Traditional Protestant (Pulpit, Guzik) | Baptist (Spurgeon) | Reformed Baptist (Piper) | Dispensational (Constable) | Modern Critical (Ellicott) | Catholic/Patristic (Augustine) |
|-------|------|-----|------|------|------|------|
| **Who speaks?** | David primarily; Christ in v.10 | Christ throughout | David, with messianic fulfillment | David only | David only | Christ throughout |
| **v.10 "see corruption"** | Refers to resurrection; LXX "corruption" is correct | Christ's literal resurrection | David's hope of preservation through death | David's hope he wouldn't die *at that time* | Hebrew *shachath* = "pit," not "corruption" | Christ's body would not decay |
| **Resurrection in OT?** | A clear OT hope, beyond Job | Christ's resurrection prophesied | Genuine OT hope of life beyond death | David only expected temporary deliverance | "First faint scintillation" of immortality | Fully realized only in Christ |
